entry.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
entry.summary: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.
entry.arxiv:comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, accepted at the 13th IEEE Special Session Privacy and Security of Big Data of IEEE BigData 2026

entry.title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
entry.summary: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://github.com/kyotovision-public/bal

entry.title: Reconstruction of Dynamical Dark Energy and Gravity from latest cosmological data
entry.summary: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in non-standard late-time evolution. We investigate whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark energy density, $Ω_{\rm X}(a)$, and the gravitational response functions $μ(a)$ and $Σ(a)$. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+, and large scale structure observations, including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data, we perform reconstructions with and without a theory motivated correlation prior derived from stable Horndeski models. We find a persistent maximum in $Ω_{\rm X}$ at $z\simeq0.5$--$0.7$, corresponding to a crossing of the effective phantom divide. This feature is already present in the CMB+BAO combination and remains robust when modifications to clustering and lensing are allowed. The reconstructed gravitational response exhibits suggestive enhancements in $μ$ and $Σ$ over approximately the same redshift range, although these departures are less significant. Including LSS information instead favours a reduced lensing response, $Σ<1$, while leaving the background feature largely unchanged. An interpretation within Generalized Brans-Dicke theories illustrates how modifications to the effective gravitational coupling and a scalar-mediated fifth force may contribute to these trends. Our results indicate that current departures from $Λ$CDM are most significant in the expansion history, while leaving open the possibility of correlated modifications to gravitational dynamics that future Stage IV surveys can test.

entry.title: Does Dark Energy Evolve $\textit{and}$ Cluster?
entry.summary: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in dynamical dark energy, and naturally raise the question of whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics. We address this question through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark-energy contribution to the expansion and the gravitational responses governing clustering and lensing, complemented by a combined covariance-mode analysis, without imposing model-specific relations between the sectors. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ supernova observations, and subsequently adding large scale structure observations including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data and other surveys, we recover a broad maximum in the effective dark-energy density near $z\simeq0.6$--$0.7$. The gravitational responses exhibit suggestive low-redshift enhancements over their GR values, approximately coincident with the background feature. Adding large scale structure information preserves the background feature but favours a mildly reduced lensing response. The combined covariance-mode analysis identifies the combinations of background and gravitational responses most tightly constrained by current observations and quantifies their departures from $Λ$CDM. The leading modes are decisively background dominated, while the gravitational sector remains less precisely constrained. Thus, present data cannot yet determine whether the suggestive low-redshift features in the two sectors share a common physical origin, a question that ongoing Stage-IV surveys will be able to address

entry.title: Towards invertibility of derived categories of sheaf-theoretic line operators
entry.summary: We investigate when the braided monoidal $\infty$-categories of sheaf-theoretic line operators of $3$-dimensional topological quantum field theories are invertible in the higher Morita category, so that they determine invertible $4$-dimensional anomaly theories. We consider a zoo of different examples which are inherently derived. First, enhancing Ben-Zvi--Francis--Nadler, we show that a symmetric monoidal category of quasi-coherent sheaves $\mathrm{QC}(X)$ is invertible only if $X$ is a point, and convolution categories on loop stacks are Morita trivial whenever the stack satisfies descent along its diagonal, e.g. for classifying stacks. Secondly, we provide an example showing that, unlike for finite braided tensor categories, non-degeneracy does not imply invertibility in the derived setting: For an odd vector space $V[1]$, the $2$-shifted $\mathcal{D}$-modules $\mathrm{DMod}^2(V[1])$ are $3$-dualizable and non-degenerate but neither factorizable nor cofactorizable. This category is closely related to the line operators of linear Rozansky--Witten theory. Finally, we define an anomaly of a group action on an invertible braided monoidal $\infty$-category as a Witt class over $\mathrm{Rep}(G)$, and show that the category of representations of the quantum group of a torus at a root of unity is invertible relative to its quantum Frobenius.

entry.title: Real-time simulation of scattering in $φ^4$ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts
entry.summary: Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in $φ^4$ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulation of scattering.

entry.title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple
entry.summary: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

entry.title: Polynomial-Time Solvability of the Multi-Dimensional Slope Change Problem
entry.summary: Slope change detection seeks to identify changes in the trends of time-ordered signals. We study the problem of fitting a multidimensional time series by continuous piecewise-linear functions with a shared continuous breakpoint and unrestricted slopes. We consider both the dense setting, in which every dimension may change slope, and the sparse setting, in which at most $k$ dimensions may change slope. Although the resulting optimization problems are nonconvex mixed integer nonlinear programs and may have irrational optimal solutions even for rational data, we prove that all six variants, corresponding to the $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_\infty$ losses in both settings, are exactly solvable in polynomial time. For least-squares loss, we obtain efficient algorithms requiring $O(JT)$ operations in the dense setting and $O(J^2T\log J)$ operations in the sparse setting, where $T$ is the number of time points and $J$ is the number of dimensions. We implement these least-squares algorithms and evaluate them on simulated data and three real-world time series, namely, surface temperatures (ERA5), hand-tracking data from a mixed-reality headset (HoloAssist), and turbofan engine sensor data (NASA C-MAPSS). The dense algorithm solves instances with up to $J=10^5$ and $T=100$, that is, $10^7$ observations, in less than $0.1$ seconds on a laptop, while the sparse algorithm solves instances with about $10^3$ dimensions and up to $T=240$ in under a second. Compared with a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) formulation solved by Gurobi, our algorithms are several orders of magnitude faster (approximately $8.9 \times 10^3$ to $3.4 \times 10^6$ times) on instances where Gurobi terminates within its default optimality tolerance of $0.01\%$ optimality gap. On larger instances, Gurobi frequently reaches a 10,000-second time limit with substantial optimality gaps.

entry.title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
entry.summary: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted for publication in International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR). 21 pages, 18 figures

entry.title: From smoothed analysis to backward error: The power of adaptive perturbations
entry.summary: Smoothed analysis has become a central tool in theoretical computer science, often allowing for significant improvements to worst-case running times if we settle for a solution to a small random perturbation of the problem instance. This is closely related to the classical concept of backward error in numerical analysis, which allows an algorithm to return a solution to an arbitrary perturbation of the problem. Despite the qualitative similarity of these concepts, we show that they can exhibit large quantitative differences. Notably, we prove that, while a linear system with any $n \times n$ matrix $A$ can be solved to backward error $ε$ using $O(\log(n) / ε)$ matrix-vector products with $A$, any algorithm that solves a random $ε$-sized perturbation of $A$ requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products. This means that a useful perturbation for solving a linear system in backward error must be adaptive to the input. Interestingly, however, randomness is still essential: we show that any deterministic method that attains small backward error for all linear systems provably requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products, resulting in the first separation between randomized and deterministic algorithms in a natural computational model for solving linear systems. Finally, we show that matrix structure can significantly affect backward error complexity. For example, we show a deterministic $O(1/ε)$ matrix-vector product algorithm for symmetric linear systems.

entry.title: Tight Bounds for k-Median++ and Improved Bounds for k-Means++
entry.summary: The popular $k$-means++ algorithm, or $D^\ell$-sampling, is a fundamental primitive in both the theory and practice of clustering. In the bi-criteria setting, the algorithm samples $k+Δ$ centers ($Δ\ge0$), and its cost is compared with the optimum using $k$ centers. Despite extensive study over the past two decades, its exact approximation ratio and tight bi-criteria guarantees remain unknown. We give a unified analysis for every distance exponent $\ell>0$, every $k\ge1$, and every $Δ\ge0$. For metric $k$-median, our bounds are tight for all $k$ and $Δ$. Without extra centers, the exact approximation ratio is $2(1+H_{k-1})$ (also in Euclidean space), improving the previous upper bound by a factor of $2$ ($H_j$ denotes the $j$th harmonic number). This tight analysis reveals that even one extra center improves the approximation ratio by an additive $Θ(\log\log k)$, whereas previous bounds show no improvement. For every $\ell>0$, our analysis gives upper bounds with the same dependence on $k$ and $Δ$ as our tight bound for metric $k$-median, with leading constants depending only on $\ell$ and whether the metric is Euclidean. Beyond the improved dependence on $Δ$, our leading constants are smaller than those in previous analyses. In particular, for the widely used Euclidean $k$-means objective, our upper bound without extra centers is $(1+\varphi)(1+H_{k-1})$, where $\varphi\approx1.618$ is the golden ratio, improving upon the previous constant of $5$. With oversampling, a constant fraction of extra centers is known to provide a constant-factor approximation. For example, with $10\%$ extra centers, our guarantee is $5.7$, compared with the best previous guarantee of $25.9$.

entry.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
entry.summary: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

entry.title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)
entry.summary: No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $Θ_0, Θ_1, Θ_2, \dots$ with $Θ_k \circ Θ_j = Θ_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $Θ_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two. Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.
entry.arxiv:comment: 59 pages, 13 figures; the main theorem is checked in Agda; the formal development is available at https://github.com/ualib/agda-deans-problem

entry.title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
entry.summary: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.

entry.title: A Surrogate Boundary Condition for Improved Accuracy and Performance of Local Modeling in Radiation Transport Simulations
entry.summary: Monte Carlo neutronics analysis of tokamak designs is computationally expensive due to the complex CAD geometries required to accurately model them. Design iteration of port plugs using global transport in the full model is impractical because of the computational cost. To circumvent this, local modeling methods are used. In the local modeling method, a boundary condition is assumed on the port plug, such that particles that leave the port plug do not require transport in the surrounding global model. For this purpose, vacuum and reflective boundaries are assumed, both of which provide poor approximation of the true transport physics in the global model. To improve on current techniques, a surrogate model is presented that provides a physics-informed boundary condition for the component. A neural network is trained to reproduce the boundary condition on the component that represents the behavior of particles returning from the surrounding geometry. Monte Carlo transport is only necessary within the component, and approximate physics from the surrounding region are retained. This approach allows the design in the component to be iterated without requiring full model transport and joining of the component mesh to the global mesh in each iteration. In this work, the surrogate model is evaluated against vacuum and reflective boundaries-- outperforming both in accuracy, with surrogate predictions of the flux in the port plug differing less than 12% from the global transport solution in any given energy bin. The surrogate boundary condition is also demonstrated to be more performant than global transport for the simplified benchmark geometry.
